Accounts are numbers
How does the Linux kernel identify the owner of a file?
By a numeric UID
By the owner's login name stored inside the file itself
By the full path of the owner's home directory on disk
By the hostname of the machine on which the file was created
The kernel stores numeric UIDs and GIDs; names are looked up in /etc/passwd and /etc/group for display.
m
Account files
Which file holds password hashes on a modern Linux system?
/etc/shadow
/etc/passwd, in its second colon-separated field
/etc/group, in the field after the group's name
/var/log/auth.log, written at each successful login
/etc/passwd shows x in the password field; hashes live in /etc/shadow, readable only by root.
d
UID 0
An audit finds a second account in /etc/passwd with UID 0. Why is this serious?
Any UID 0 account has full root privileges
It means the account was created by the kernel during installation
It prevents the real root account from logging in at the console
It shows the account has been locked and can safely be ignored
Privilege follows the UID, not the name. An extra UID 0 account is a classic backdoor.
m
Locking accounts
What is the effect of passwd -l on an account?
It locks password login by invalidating the stored hash
It deletes the account and its home directory from the system
It forces the user to choose a new password at the next login only
It removes the account from every group except its primary group
Locking prefixes the hash so password authentication fails. Other methods, such as SSH keys, may still work unless also disabled.
d
Service accounts
Why do service accounts often have /usr/sbin/nologin as their shell?
So they cannot be used for interactive logins
So their processes run faster without a shell environment loaded
So that their files are hidden from directory listings by other users
So that the package manager can update them without any password
A non-login shell stops someone from obtaining an interactive session as the service account, while the service still runs.
m
Octal permissions
What permissions does chmod 750 script.sh give?
Owner rwx, group r-x, others none
Owner rw-, group r--, others r--
Owner rwx, group rwx, others r-x
Owner r-x, group rw-, others none
7 = rwx, 5 = r-x, 0 = ---, applied to owner, group and others.
m
Symbolic notation
Which command removes write permission for others from report.txt?
chmod o-w report.txt
chmod u+w report.txt
chown others report.txt
chmod 777 report.txt
o-w removes write from others. u+w adds write for the owner, and 777 grants everything to everyone.
d
Directory permissions
On a directory, what does the write permission allow?
Creating, deleting and renaming entries in it
Changing the contents of the files inside it, even without file write permission
Listing the names of the files it contains without any other permission
Entering the directory with cd and reading files inside it
Directory write permission controls entries (names). Read lists names, and execute allows traversal.
d
umask
With a umask of 027, what permissions does a newly created regular file get by default?
Files start from 666; masking 027 removes group write and all permissions for others, giving 640.
m
Ownership
What does chown alice:finance budget.xlsx do?
Sets the owner to alice and the group to finance
Gives alice and finance members full permissions
Copies the file to alice's home directory
Adds alice to the finance group permanently
chown changes owner and group; permission bits are changed with chmod.
d
setgid on directories
A shared folder /srv/team has the setgid bit set. What does that change?
New files inherit the directory's group
New files are owned by root regardless of who creates them
Only the group owner can create new files inside it
Files inside it run with the group's privileges
setgid on a directory makes new entries inherit its group, which keeps team folders consistently shared.
m
Sticky bit
Why does /tmp have the sticky bit set?
So users can delete only their own files there
So files in it survive a reboot of the system
So only root can write new files into it
So files in it execute with the owner's rights
The sticky bit restricts deletion and renaming in a shared, world-writable directory to the file's owner (and root).
d
SUID audit
Why do hardening audits list all SUID binaries with find / -perm -4000?
Each one runs with its owner's rights, often root, and is a potential escalation path
SUID binaries cannot be patched, so they must be removed after every upgrade
SUID binaries use more memory, so the list helps capacity planning
SUID binaries are always malware, so every result must be deleted
Unexpected or vulnerable SUID-root programs are a common local privilege escalation route.
m
POSIX ACLs
Which command grants user ravi read access to a file without changing its owner or group?
setfacl -m u:ravi:r file
chmod ravi+r file
chown ravi file
usermod -r file ravi
setfacl adds an access control entry for one user; getfacl shows the result.
d
Beyond DAC
What does mandatory access control such as SELinux add to standard Linux permissions?
A system-wide policy that confines processes even when file permissions would allow access
A replacement for user passwords based on hardware security keys only
A backup copy of every file that the kernel restores after changes
A way for normal users to grant themselves root without sudo
MAC policies confine what each process may do, so a compromised service is limited even if it runs as root.
m
Why sudo
Why is sudo preferred to sharing the root password?
Each action is tied to an individual and can be limited
sudo runs commands faster than a root shell does
sudo encrypts every command before the kernel sees it
sudo needs no configuration on any distribution
sudo gives per-user accountability (logged actions) and lets policy restrict which commands each person may run.
d
sudoers grammar
What does the sudoers line 'ops ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx' allow?
Members' account ops to restart nginx as root, and nothing else via that rule
The ops account to run any systemctl command on any service as root
Every user on the system to restart nginx without a password
The ops account to edit the nginx configuration file as root
The rule is narrow: one user, run as root, one exact command with those arguments.
d
Editing sudoers
Why should sudoers be edited with visudo?
It checks syntax before saving, avoiding a lockout
It encrypts the file so that other users cannot read it
It is the only editor that root is allowed to run
It automatically grants the editor sudo rights
A syntax error in sudoers can break sudo entirely; visudo validates the file first.
m
SSH basics
Which sshd_config setting stops direct root logins over SSH?
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication yes
Port 2222
X11Forwarding yes
PermitRootLogin no forces administrators to log in as themselves and elevate, which preserves accountability.
m
Package management
Why should software be installed from the distribution's package manager rather than downloaded installers?
Packages are signed and receive security updates centrally
Downloaded installers cannot run on Linux at all
Package managers install software without using any disk space
Packages never need a restart after they are updated
Signed repositories give integrity and a single update path, which is the basis of patch management.
d
Repository trust
What does GPG signature checking of a repository protect against?
Tampered or substituted packages from a compromised mirror
Vulnerabilities in the code written by the original developers
Users installing software they are not authorised to use
Disk corruption on the local system after installation
Signatures prove packages came from the key holder unchanged. They do not prove the code is free of bugs.
d
Verifying installed files
rpm -V or debsums reports a changed checksum for /usr/bin/ls. What should a responder conclude?
The binary differs from the packaged version and must be investigated
The package manager has a bug and the report should be ignored
The file was updated by a routine security patch, which is normal
The file system is full and the checksum could not be computed
Package verification compares installed files with package metadata. A changed system binary may indicate tampering.
m
Patch practice
Which order reflects sound patch management?
Inventory, assess, test, deploy in stages, verify
Deploy everywhere, then test whether anything broke
Wait for an incident, then patch the affected host
Test once a year, then deploy every update at once
A defined cycle with testing and staged rollout balances security with stability.
m
systemd journal
Which command shows journal entries for the sshd unit since yesterday?
journalctl -u sshd --since yesterday
systemctl log sshd yesterday
tail -u sshd /var/log/journal
dmesg --unit sshd --since 1
journalctl filters by unit with -u and by time with --since.
d
Journal persistence
Why might journal logs disappear after a reboot on some systems?
The journal is kept only in memory unless persistent storage is configured
journald deletes all logs at every boot for privacy reasons
Rebooting rotates every log into an encrypted archive automatically
systemd writes logs only while a user is logged in
Without /var/log/journal (or Storage=persistent), the journal lives in /run and is lost at reboot.
d
Log rotation
Why must log rotation settings be considered in incident response planning?
Rotation deletes old logs on a schedule, so evidence may expire before it is needed
Rotation encrypts logs, so responders need the key to read them later
Rotation stops logging entirely while the archive is being created
Rotation copies logs to every user's home directory by default
logrotate keeps a set number of old files. Forwarding to a central store protects evidence beyond local retention.
